```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

Adding a joinpoint almost always improves the fit (not always: placement
rules can exclude the best location of an extra joinpoint), so the number
of joinpoints has to be chosen by a rule that weighs fit against
complexity.
The permutation test of Kim et al. (2000) was long the standard; the
weighted BIC (WBIC) of Kim et al. (2023) reaches similar answers in a
fraction of the time. Applied to the same data, different rules can give
different numbers of joinpoints, and analysts wonder which answer to
trust. This vignette shows what each rule does, reproduces a
published permutation test analysis, and shows how to remove joinpoints that
are statistically detectable but too small to matter.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The candidates

For every number of joinpoints from `kmin` to `kmax`, `joinpoint()` finds
the best fitting model by an exhaustive grid search. Model selection only
chooses among these best fits. `plot_models()` shows them side by side for
one cohort, with the criterion of each model in its title.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
stroke <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Stroke")
fit <- joinpoint(stroke, year, rate, kmax = 4, ci_method = "parametric")
plot_models(fit, ncol = 3)
```

## Information criteria

The BIC family has the form `ln(SSE / n) + penalty(k) ln(n) / n`:

- **BIC** uses the penalty `2k + 2` (intercept, slope, `k` slope changes and
  `k` locations). It detects small changes but tends to over fit.
- **BIC3** uses the harsher `3k + 2` and behaves like the permutation test.
- **WBIC**, the package default, mixes the two with a weight
  equal to the largest local partial R^2 of a slope change, so clear changes
  are penalized like BIC3 and subtle ones like BIC (Kim et al. 2023).
- **Modified BIC** (Zhang and Siegmund 2007) adds to the BIC terms for the
  determinant of the design and the residual sum of squares; it is the
  most conservative.
- **Data dependent selection** (DDS) picks between the BIC and BIC3 answers
  using the size of the detected changes.

`plot_selection()` draws the criteria against the number of joinpoints.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_selection(fit)
```

The answers differ across causes and methods:

```{r}
methods <- c("bic", "bic3", "wbic", "mbic", "dds")
k <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
  f <- joinpoint(us_mortality, year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 4,
                 method = m, ci_method = "parametric")
  model_selection(f)$selected$joinpoints
})
rownames(k) <- levels(us_mortality$cause)
k
```

With 99 years of precise data, most criteria use all four joinpoints
allowed: the changes are large relative to the noise. The modified BIC is
far more conservative for accidents and cancer, and for influenza and
pneumonia only BIC keeps four joinpoints. BIC never selects fewer joinpoints
than BIC3 because its penalty is smaller for every `k`. Where the methods
agree the answer is robust; where they disagree, the extra joinpoints of the
liberal criteria mark modest changes that deserve cautious interpretation.

## The permutation test

The permutation test (Kim et al. 2000) tests `k = a` joinpoints against
`k = b` sequentially, starting from `a = kmin` and `b = kmax`: a rejection
raises `a`, otherwise `b` falls, until the two meet. Each test permutes the
residuals of the null model, refits both models to every permuted data set,
and uses the level `alpha / (kmax - a)` to keep the overall probability of
over fitting below `alpha`.

A published tutorial (van Doren 2024) analyzed the mortality data with
linear models, at most three joinpoints and the permutation test with 4499
permutations, and selected one joinpoint for influenza and pneumonia and
three for every other cause. The package reproduces these selections:

```{r}
fit_perm <- joinpoint(us_mortality, year, rate, by = "cause", log = FALSE,
                      kmax = 3, method = "permutation",
                      ci_method = "parametric")
model_selection(fit_perm)$selected[, c("cause", "joinpoints")]
```

The sequence of tests shows why influenza and pneumonia stopped at one
joinpoint: the test of one against two joinpoints gave a p value just above
its level of 0.025.

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot_selection(fit_perm)
```

Permutation p values are Monte Carlo estimates, so a p value close to its
level can fall on either side with another seed; more permutations reduce
the Monte Carlo error but cannot settle a p value that truly sits at the
level. Report such borderline decisions as such, and use the WBIC when
computing time matters.

## Joinpoints too small to matter

With long, precise series even small changes of slope can become
statistically significant. The minimum APC difference worth detecting (MADWD) is a
substantive filter applied after selection: if any two adjacent segments
differ by less than the threshold (in percentage points), the best model
with one joinpoint fewer is taken, until all adjacent segments pass.

```{r}
fit_madwd <- joinpoint(stroke, year, rate, kmax = 4, method = "bic",
                       ci_method = "parametric",
                       control = jp_control(madwd = 2))
model_selection(fit_madwd)$madwd
```

With a threshold of 2 percentage points, the four and three joinpoint
models fail because two adjacent segments differ by less than that, and the
two joinpoint model is kept. Choose the threshold before looking at the
results; changing it until the
trends look as expected defeats its purpose.

## References

Kim HJ, Fay MP, Feuer EJ, Midthune DN (2000). Permutation tests for
joinpoint regression with applications to cancer rates. *Statistics in
Medicine* 19:335-351.

Kim HJ, Chen HS, Midthune D, et al. (2023). Data-driven choice of a model
selection method in joinpoint regression. *Journal of Applied Statistics*
50:1992-2013.

van Doren T (2024). Estimating time points of significant change in
cause-specific mortality: joinpoint regression in R. *The Denominator*.
doi:10.6069/JK1Y-7Z16

Zhang NR, Siegmund DO (2007). A modified Bayes information criterion with
applications to the analysis of comparative genomic hybridization data.
*Biometrics* 63:22-32.
